newsitem.title: USA: Texaco annual meeting hit by protests.
newsitem.headline: Texaco annual meeting hit by protests.

text.p: Texaco Inc.'s annual shareholder meeting on Tuesday was a magnet for those criticising the company on racial and environmental grounds and for its investment in Burma.

Instead of gathering to discuss the company's proposed stock split, shareholders in the White Plains, N.Y., oil company were treated to banners and placards calling Texaco "The star destroyer of the forests," referring to the company logo and its alleged pollution of the rainforest in Ecuador.
"The oil they spilled is lying in pools in the forests. Texaco had the technology to clean the spills up, but did not use it," said James Hansen of the Rainforest Action Group.

Texaco denies it caused pollution and recently won the first round of a billion dollar lawsuit in U.S. District Court in New York, which environmentalists and the government of Ecuador have submitted for reconsideration.
Among the 40 protestors gathered outside the Rye Hilton, the Reverend Jesse Jackson's Rainbow-Push coalition demanded more women and minorities in management.
Texaco last year settled a racial discrimination lawsuit for $115 million plus an 11.4 percent increase in salaries for plaintiffs.
Texaco settled the 1996 suit rather than continue litigation after transcripts of tape recordings showed executives allegedly discussing the destruction of documents and making racist remarks.
The company said it had implemented a programme to ensure fairness in the treatment of ethnic minorities and women.

"Arbitrary deadlines could sacrifice the thoroughess of this effort. All of this activity occurs of necessity behind the scenes, where the level and intensity of the effort cannot be apparent to stockholders," Texaco said in response.

Protestors are also angry that Texaco has not divested its 43 percent stake in a natural gas field in the Andaman Sea, off the coast of Burma, which they say is giving succor to Burma's military government.

Texaco shareholders overwhelmingly rejected a call to get out of Burma last year and the company has always said it will obey U.S. law, which was recently changed to halt new, but not existing investment in Burma.
